html:
On the morning of 17 August 1945 Sukarno read a short declaration of independence for Indonesia outside his house in Jakarta, with Mohammad Hatta beside him. It was two days after Japan announced its surrender.

Japan had conquered the Dutch East Indies in early 1942 and ended more than three centuries of Dutch presence. The occupation was harsh, with forced labour and famine, but it also trained young Indonesians in arms and let nationalist leaders speak to the masses. With Japan beaten after the atomic bombings and the Soviet entry into the war, young radicals pressed Sukarno and Hatta to act before the Allies arrived. They even took the two leaders out of the city the night before to push them.

The text was only two sentences. It declared independence and said the transfer of power would be carried out carefully and as quickly as possible. The next day Sukarno and Hatta were named president and vice-president.

The Dutch did not accept it. British troops landed first, and the Battle of Surabaya in November 1945 showed how hard Indonesians would fight. Four years of war and talks followed, the Indonesian National Revolution, until the Netherlands transferred sovereignty in December 1949.

17 August is Indonesia's national day. The Netherlands formally recognised 1945 as the date of independence only in 2023. The declaration opened the wave of independence across Southeast Asia.
